chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text:
- A CIRCLE is a collection of all points in a plane which are at a constant distance (RADIUS) from a fixed point (CENTRE).
- A TANGENT to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at only one point.
- A SECANT is a line that intersects a circle at two distinct points.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: When a line and a circle are given in a plane, there are exactly THREE possible positions:
(i) The line does not intersect the circle (NON-INTERSECTING LINE).
(ii) The line intersects the circle at two points (SECANT).
(iii) The line touches the circle at exactly one point (TANGENT).
The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the POINT OF CONTACT.
A tangent is a special case of a secant — when the two end points of the corresponding chord coincide.
The tangent at any point is PERPENDICULAR to the radius at the point of contact.
From an EXTERNAL POINT, exactly TWO tangents of EQUAL LENGTH can be drawn.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
- A CIRCLE is a collection of all points in a plane which are at a constant distance (called the RADIUS) from a fixed point (called the CENTRE).
- When a circle and a line are in the same plane, the line is called a NON-INTERSECTING LINE, SECANT, or TANGENT depending on the number of common points.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Terms already studied in Class IX related to circles: chord, segment, sector, arc, radius, diameter, centre.
THREE cases for a line PQ and a circle in a plane:
Case (i): Line PQ has NO common point with the circle → NON-INTERSECTING LINE.
Case (ii): Line PQ has TWO common points A and B → SECANT of the circle.
Case (iii): Line PQ has exactly ONE common point A → TANGENT to the circle.
The tangent is said to TOUCH the circle at the common point (POINT OF CONTACT).
Real-life example: The rope on both sides of a pulley acts like a TANGENT to the circle of the pulley.
There is NO fourth possibility — only these three cases exist.
In this chapter: existence of tangents and their properties are studied.
(No sub-topics in 10.1 — Mode B)

items.question: What is a circle? Define secant and tangent.
items.answer:
CIRCLE: A collection of all points in a plane which are at a constant distance (RADIUS) from a fixed point (CENTRE).
SECANT: A line intersecting a circle at two distinct common points.
TANGENT: A line intersecting a circle at exactly one point — that point is called the POINT OF CONTACT.

items.question: What are the three possible positions of a line with respect to a circle?
items.answer:
(i) NON-INTERSECTING LINE: No common point with the circle.
(ii) SECANT: Two common points with the circle.
(iii) TANGENT: Exactly one common point with the circle (point of contact).
There is no fourth possibility.

items.question: Name one real-life example each of a tangent and a secant to a circle.
items.answer:
TANGENT: The rope on both sides of a pulley acts like a tangent to the circle of the pulley. Also, the ground under a bicycle wheel acts as a tangent.
SECANT: A straight cut across a circular pizza — the cutting line intersects the circle at two points.

items.question: What is the point of contact? Can a line intersect a circle at more than two points?
items.answer:
POINT OF CONTACT: The single common point of a tangent and a circle. The tangent is said to touch the circle at this point.
No — a line can intersect a circle at most at two points. The only three cases are: zero (non-intersecting), one (tangent), or two (secant) common points.

---

3 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 3 questions:

items.question: Explain the three cases that arise when a circle and a line are given in a plane. Give one real-life example.
items.answer:
Step 1: CASE (i) — NON-INTERSECTING LINE (Fig. 10.1(i)):
Line PQ has no common point with the circle. The line lies entirely outside.
Step 2: CASE (ii) — SECANT (Fig. 10.1(ii)):
Line PQ has two common points A and B with the circle. It cuts through the circle.
Step 3: CASE (iii) — TANGENT (Fig. 10.1(iii)):
Line PQ has exactly one common point A. It touches the circle. A is the point of contact.
Real-life example: The rope on a pulley (Fig. 10.2) behaves like a tangent — touching the circular pulley at one point on each side.

items.question: How is a tangent related to a secant? Describe Activity 10.2.1.
items.answer:
A tangent is a SPECIAL CASE (limiting case) of a secant — when both end points of the corresponding chord coincide.
Step 1: In Activity 10.2.1, a wire AB is attached at point P on a circular wire and rotated.
Step 2: In most positions, AB intersects the circle at P and at another point — acting as a secant.
Step 3: As AB rotates, the second intersection point moves closer to P. In one unique position, it coincides with P — AB intersects the circle only at P. This is the TANGENT at P.
Conclusion: The tangent to a circle is the secant when the two end points of the corresponding chord coincide.

items.question: What does Activity 10.2.2 establish? State two conclusions from it.
items.answer:
Activity 10.2.2 draws lines parallel to a secant PQ on both sides of it.
Step 1: As lines move away from PQ toward the boundary, the chord length cut by each line gradually decreases — the two intersection points come closer.
Step 2: On one side, chord length reaches zero — the line just touches the circle at one point. This is tangent P'Q', parallel to PQ.
Step 3: On the other side, another tangent P''Q'' is formed.
Two conclusions:
(i) A tangent is the limiting case of a secant when the chord length becomes zero.
(ii) There are at most TWO tangents parallel to a given secant.

---

4 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 4 questions:

items.question: Explain in detail the three situations arising when a line and a circle are in a plane. State which situation produces a tangent and why the tangent is a special case of a secant.
items.answer:
Step 1: NON-INTERSECTING LINE:
When the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line is greater than the radius, the line has no common point with the circle. It is a non-intersecting line.
Step 2: SECANT:
When the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line is less than the radius, the line intersects the circle at two points A and B. The line is a SECANT of the circle.
Step 3: TANGENT:
When the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line exactly equals the radius, the line touches the circle at exactly one point A. The line is a TANGENT. Point A is the POINT OF CONTACT.
Step 4: Why is tangent a special case of secant?
As a secant moves parallel to itself (Activity 10.2.2), the chord length decreases. When it reaches zero, the two intersection points coincide at one point — the secant becomes a tangent. So a tangent is a secant whose chord length has become zero — i.e., a special limiting case.
Real-life: A bicycle wheel moving on the ground — the ground is tangent to the wheel at the single point of contact at any moment.

items.question: Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm. The chord AB of the larger circle touches the smaller circle. Find AB and prove that AB is bisected at the point of contact.
items.answer:
Given: Larger circle C1 (radius OA = 5 cm), smaller circle C2 (radius OP = 3 cm), same centre O. AB is a chord of C1 tangent to C2 at P.
To Find: AB. To Prove: AP = PB.
Step 1: AB is a tangent to C2 at P. OP is the radius of C2.
By Theorem 10.1: OP ⊥ AB.
Step 2: OP is perpendicular to chord AB of circle C1 from centre O.
By perpendicular-from-centre property: OP bisects AB → AP = PB.
HENCE PROVED that AB is bisected at P.
Step 3: In right triangle OAP:
AP² = OA² − OP² = 25 − 9 = 16 → AP = 4 cm.
Step 4: AB = 2 × AP = 8 cm.
Answer: AB = 8 cm. The chord is bisected at the point of contact P.

items.question: A line PQ is such that the perpendicular distance from the centre O is: (i) greater than r, (ii) equal to r, (iii) less than r. For each case state what PQ is called, and give the number of common points.
items.answer:
Step 1: CASE (i) — Perpendicular distance > radius r:
PQ has NO common point with the circle.
PQ is called a NON-INTERSECTING LINE with respect to the circle.
Number of common points: 0.

Step 2: CASE (ii) — Perpendicular distance = radius r:
PQ has exactly ONE common point with the circle.
PQ is called a TANGENT to the circle.
Number of common points: 1 (the point of contact).

Step 3: CASE (iii) — Perpendicular distance < radius r:
PQ has TWO common points with the circle.
PQ is called a SECANT of the circle.
Number of common points: 2.

Step 4: Summary table:
d > r → Non-intersecting → 0 points.
d = r → Tangent → 1 point.
d < r → Secant → 2 points.
(Where d = perpendicular distance from centre O to line PQ, r = radius.)

items.question: A student says: "A tangent and a secant have nothing in common." Correct this statement and show the connection between them using both Activity 10.2.1 and Activity 10.2.2.
items.answer:
The student's statement is INCORRECT. A tangent is actually a special limiting case of a secant.
Step 1: Connection via Activity 10.2.1 (Rotating wire):
Wire AB rotates about point P on the circle. In most positions it intersects at P and another point — it is a secant. As it rotates, the second intersection point moves closer to P. In one position, both points coincide at P — the wire becomes a TANGENT. Conclusion: tangent = secant when both chord end points coincide.
Step 2: Connection via Activity 10.2.2 (Parallel lines):
Lines parallel to secant PQ are drawn. As lines shift toward the edge of the circle, the chord length decreases. When chord length = 0, the line touches the circle at one point — it becomes a TANGENT. Conclusion: tangent = secant when chord length → 0.
Step 3: Formal statement from textbook:
"The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end points of its corresponding chord coincide."
Step 4: Also: a circle can have at most TWO tangents parallel to any given secant — one on each side. This further connects the two concepts.

---

5 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 1 question:

PART A — Three Cases of Line and Circle:

Case 1 — NON-INTERSECTING LINE:
The line has NO common point with the circle.
The perpendicular distance from centre O to the line > radius.
Number of common points: 0.
Real-life: A road passing at a safe distance from a circular pond — it does not touch or cross the pond.

Case 2 — SECANT:
The line intersects the circle at TWO distinct common points A and B.
The perpendicular distance from centre O to the line < radius.
The line is called a SECANT of the circle.
Number of common points: 2.
Real-life: A straight cut across a circular disc — enters at one point and exits at another.

Case 3 — TANGENT:
The line has exactly ONE common point with the circle — the POINT OF CONTACT.
The perpendicular distance from centre O to the line = radius.
The line is called a TANGENT to the circle.
Number of common points: 1.
Real-life: A bicycle wheel on the road — the road is tangent to the wheel at the single ground-contact point. Also, the rope on a pulley (Fig. 10.2).

Key note: A tangent is a SPECIAL CASE of the secant — when the chord's two end points coincide (chord length → 0). There are exactly two tangents parallel to any given secant (one on each side).

---

PART B — Proof and Calculation:

Given: Larger circle C1 (radius OA = 10 cm), smaller circle C2 (radius OP = 6 cm), common centre O. Chord AB of C1 touches C2 at P.
To Prove: AP = PB.
To Find: Length of AB.

Step 1: AB is a tangent to circle C2 at point P.
OP is the radius of C2 at the point of contact P.
Step 2: By Theorem 10.1: OP ⊥ AB (radius is perpendicular to tangent at point of contact).
Step 3: OP is the perpendicular from centre O to chord AB of circle C1.
By the property "perpendicular from centre to a chord bisects the chord":
AP = PB.
HENCE PROVED: Chord AB is bisected at its point of contact P with the smaller circle.

Step 4: In right-angled triangle OAP:
OA = 10 cm (radius of larger circle)
OP = 6 cm (radius of smaller circle)
AP² = OA² − OP² = 100 − 36 = 64
AP = 8 cm.
Step 5: AB = 2 × AP = 2 × 8 = 16 cm.
Answer: AB = 16 cm.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
- A TANGENT to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at only one point (the POINT OF CONTACT).
- The POINT OF CONTACT is the single common point of the tangent and the circle.
- The NORMAL to a circle at a point is the line containing the radius through the point of contact.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: At any point on a circle, there is ONE AND ONLY ONE tangent.
At most TWO tangents can be drawn parallel to a given secant.
The tangent to a circle is a SPECIAL CASE of the secant — when both end points of the corresponding chord coincide.
THEOREM 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is PERPENDICULAR to the radius through the point of contact.
The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also called the NORMAL to the circle at that point.
"Tangent" comes from the Latin word "tangere" meaning to touch — introduced by Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583.
(No sub-topics in 10.2 — Mode B)
ACTIVITY 10.2.1: Rotating Wire Activity
AIM: To show that exactly one tangent exists at any point on a circle.
MATERIALS: Circular wire, straight wire AB, table.
PROCEDURE:
Attach straight wire AB at point P on the circular wire so it can rotate about P.
Gently rotate AB about point P to get different positions.
OBSERVATION:
In most positions, AB intersects the circle at P and at another point Q1 or Q2 or Q3, etc.
In exactly ONE position, AB intersects the circle only at P.
On rotating further, it again intersects at P and another point R1, R2, R3, etc.
CONCLUSION: There is ONLY ONE TANGENT at any point of the circle.
ACTIVITY 10.2.2: Parallel Lines Activity
AIM: To show that a tangent is a limiting case of a secant, and at most two tangents are parallel to a given secant.
MATERIALS: Paper, compass, ruler.
PROCEDURE:
Draw a circle and a secant PQ.
Draw various lines parallel to PQ on both sides.
OBSERVATION:
The chord length cut by parallel lines gradually decreases.
On one side, the chord length reaches zero at position P'Q' (tangent).
On the other side, it reaches zero at position P''Q'' (tangent).
CONCLUSION: A tangent is the secant when both end points of the chord coincide. There are at most TWO tangents parallel to a given secant.

sections.label: THEOREM 10.1:
sections.statement: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
sections.given: A circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a point P.
proof: Step 1: Take any point Q on XY other than P. Join OQ.
Step 2: Q must lie outside the circle. (If Q were inside, XY would be a secant, not a tangent.)
Step 3: Since Q is outside the circle, OQ > OP (OP is the radius, OQ extends beyond).
Step 4: This is true for every point on XY except P.
Step 5: Therefore, OP is the SHORTEST distance from O to line XY.
Step 6: The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance.
sections.hence_proved:
OP ⊥ XY.
REMARKS:
1. At any point on a circle, there can be ONE AND ONLY ONE tangent.
2. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also called the NORMAL to the circle at that point.
EXERCISES — EXERCISE 10.1:

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.1.1:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: How many tangents can a circle have?
SOLUTION: At each point on the circle, one tangent can be drawn. Since a circle has infinitely many points, it can have infinitely many tangents.
ANSWER: Infinitely many tangents.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.1.2: Fill in the blanks:
sections.raw:
(i) A tangent to a circle intersects it in _____ point(s).
Answer: 1
(ii) A line intersecting a circle in two points is called a _____.
Answer: Secant
(iii) A circle can have _____ parallel tangents at the most.
Answer: 2
(iv) The common point of a tangent to a circle and the circle is called _____.
Answer: Point of contact

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.1.3:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: A tangent PQ at a point P of a circle of radius 5 cm meets a line through the centre O at a point Q so that OQ = 12 cm. Find the length PQ.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1, OP ⊥ PQ, so angle OPQ = 90°.
Step 2: In right triangle OPQ:
PQ² = OQ² − OP²
PQ² = 12² − 5²
PQ² = 144 − 25 = 119
PQ = √119 cm
ANSWER: PQ = √119 cm. [Option (D)]

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.1.4:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Draw a circle and two lines parallel to a given line such that one is a tangent and the other is a secant to the circle.
SOLUTION: (Construction)
Step 1: Draw a circle with any radius.
Step 2: Draw a line l (secant) cutting the circle at two points.
Step 3: Draw a line parallel to l that touches the circle at exactly one point — this is the tangent.
Step 4: Draw another line parallel to l that cuts the circle at two points — this is the secant.
ANSWER: Construction as described above (refer Activity 10.2.2).

items.question: State Theorem 10.1 and its two remarks.
items.answer:
Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Remark 1: At any point on a circle, there can be ONE AND ONLY ONE tangent.
Remark 2: The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also called the NORMAL to the circle at that point.

items.question: How many tangents can a circle have? How many parallel tangents can a circle have?
items.answer:
A circle has INFINITELY MANY tangents — one at each of its infinitely many points.
A circle can have at most 2 PARALLEL TANGENTS (one on each side, parallel to a given secant).

items.question: What is the angle between a tangent to a circle and the radius at the point of contact? What is the "normal" to a circle?
items.answer:
The angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact is 90° (they are perpendicular to each other — Theorem 10.1).
The NORMAL to a circle at a point is the line containing the radius through the point of contact of the tangent at that point.

items.question: Exercise 10.1 Q3: A tangent PQ at P on a circle of radius 5 cm meets the line through O at Q, OQ = 12 cm. Find PQ.
items.answer:
By Theorem 10.1: angle OPQ = 90°.
In right triangle OPQ:
PQ² = OQ² − OP² = 12² − 5² = 144 − 25 = 119.
PQ = √119 cm.
Answer: PQ = √119 cm. [Option (D)]

3 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 3 questions:

items.question: Prove Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
items.answer:
Given: Circle with centre O, tangent XY at point P.
To Prove: OP ⊥ XY.
Step 1: Take any point Q on XY (Q ≠ P). Q lies outside the circle.
(If Q were inside, XY would be a secant — contradiction.)
Join OQ. Since Q is outside: OQ > OP.
Step 2: This holds for every Q on XY except P.
So OP is the SHORTEST distance from O to line XY.
Step 3: The shortest distance from a point to a line is perpendicular.
Therefore OP ⊥ XY. HENCE PROVED.

items.question: A circle has radius 8 cm. A tangent is drawn at point P. A point Q is on the tangent such that OQ = 17 cm. Find PQ.
items.answer:
Given: OP = 8 cm (radius), OQ = 17 cm, PQ is tangent at P.
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OPQ = 90°.
Step 2: In right triangle OPQ:
PQ² = OQ² − OP² = 17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225.
PQ = 15 cm.
Step 3: Verification: OP² + PQ² = 64 + 225 = 289 = OQ². ✓
Answer: PQ = 15 cm.

items.question: Why must point Q (taken on tangent XY in the proof of Theorem 10.1) lie outside the circle? What follows from this?
items.answer:
Step 1: Q is any point on tangent XY other than P.
If Q were INSIDE the circle, the line XY would pass through the interior and intersect the circle at two points — making XY a secant, not a tangent. This contradicts the given condition.
Therefore Q must lie OUTSIDE the circle.
Step 2: Since Q is outside: OQ > OP (OP is radius; OQ reaches beyond the circle to Q).
Step 3: This holds for every Q ≠ P on XY.
Therefore OP is the shortest distance from O to line XY → OP ⊥ XY.

---

4 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 4 questions:

items.question: Prove Theorem 10.1 in full, with Given, To Prove, and all proof steps. Also state what follows from the proof.
items.answer:
Given: A circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a point P.
To Prove: OP ⊥ XY.
Proof:
Step 1: Take any point Q on line XY other than P. Join OQ.
Step 2: Q must lie outside the circle.
Reason: If Q were inside, the line XY would intersect the circle at two points — making XY a secant. This contradicts the given (XY is a tangent). Hence Q is outside the circle.
Step 3: Since Q lies outside the circle: OQ > OP.
(OP is the radius; OQ extends beyond the circle to reach Q outside.)
Step 4: This is true for every point Q on XY except P itself.
Therefore OP is the SHORTEST distance from O to any point on line XY.
Step 5: The shortest distance from a point to a straight line is the perpendicular distance.
Hence OP ⊥ XY.
HENCE PROVED.
Consequence: At any point P on a circle, exactly ONE tangent can be drawn (since there is only one perpendicular from O to any line through P at the boundary). The radius through P (the normal) is perpendicular to this tangent.

items.question: Find the length of the tangent from a point A at distance 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 3 cm. Verify using Pythagoras. Also find the angle the tangent makes at the external point.
items.answer:
Given: OA = 5 cm (distance from external point A to centre O), radius OT = 3 cm (T = point of contact).
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OTA = 90°.
Step 2: In right triangle OTA:
AT² = OA² − OT² = 25 − 9 = 16.
AT = 4 cm.
Step 3: Verification (Pythagoras):
OT² + AT² = 9 + 16 = 25 = OA². ✓
Step 4: Finding angle at external point A:
cos(angle OAT) = AT/OA = 4/5.
angle OAT = cos⁻¹(4/5) ≈ 36.87°.
(Or: sin(angle OAT) = OT/OA = 3/5 → angle OAT ≈ 36.87°.)
Answer: Length of tangent AT = 4 cm. Angle at A ≈ 36.87°.

items.question: Prove that the perpendicular at the point of contact to the tangent to a circle passes through the centre. Then apply: circle of radius 6 cm, tangent at P, Q is on the tangent 8 cm from P. Find OQ.
items.answer:
Proof:
Step 1: Let XY be the tangent at P. OP is the radius at P.
Step 2: By Theorem 10.1: OP ⊥ XY.
So OP is the perpendicular to tangent XY at the point of contact P.
Step 3: The line OP passes through the centre O.
Therefore the perpendicular at the point of contact to the tangent passes through the centre.
HENCE PROVED.

Application:
Given: Radius OP = 6 cm, tangent at P, PQ = 8 cm (Q on tangent).
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OPQ = 90°.
Step 2: In right triangle OPQ:
OQ² = OP² + PQ² = 36 + 64 = 100.
OQ = 10 cm.
Answer: OQ = 10 cm.

items.question: A tangent PQ is drawn at P on a circle of radius 5 cm, centre O. Q is on the tangent such that OQ = 13 cm. Find PQ. Also find angle POQ and angle OQP.
items.answer:
Given: Radius OP = 5 cm, OQ = 13 cm, PQ tangent at P.
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OPQ = 90°.
Step 2: In right triangle OPQ:
PQ² = OQ² − OP² = 169 − 25 = 144.
PQ = 12 cm.
Step 3: Finding angle OQP:
sin(angle OQP) = OP/OQ = 5/13.
angle OQP = sin⁻¹(5/13) ≈ 22.62°.
Step 4: Finding angle POQ:
angle POQ = 180° − 90° − angle OQP = 90° − 22.62° ≈ 67.38°.
(Or: sin(angle POQ) = PQ/OQ = 12/13 → angle POQ ≈ 67.38°.)
Answer: PQ = 12 cm. angle OQP ≈ 22.62°. angle POQ ≈ 67.38°.

---

5 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 1 question:

PART A — Full Proof of Theorem 10.1:

Statement: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Given: A circle with centre O and a tangent XY at point P.
To Prove: OP ⊥ XY.

Step 1: Take any point Q on line XY, Q ≠ P. Join OQ.
Step 2: Q lies outside the circle.
(If Q were inside, XY would intersect the circle at two points → secant. Contradicts "XY is tangent".)
Step 3: OQ > OP, since Q is outside and OP is the radius.
Step 4: This holds for every Q ≠ P on XY. So OP is the shortest distance from O to XY.
Step 5: Shortest distance from a point to a line = perpendicular distance.
Therefore OP ⊥ XY.
HENCE PROVED.

Remark 1: At any point on a circle, there is ONE AND ONLY ONE tangent.
Remark 2: The line containing the radius OP through the point of contact is called the NORMAL to the circle at P.

---

PART B — Two Applications:

(i) Tangent PQ at P, radius OP = 5 cm, OQ = 12 cm. Find PQ:
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OPQ = 90°.
Step 2: PQ² = OQ² − OP² = 144 − 25 = 119 → PQ = √119 cm.
Verification: OP² + PQ² = 25 + 119 = 144 = OQ². ✓
Answer: PQ = √119 cm.

(ii) External point A, OA = 13 cm, radius OT = 5 cm, T = point of contact. Find AT:
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OTA = 90°.
Step 2: AT² = OA² − OT² = 169 − 25 = 144 → AT = 12 cm.
Verification: OT² + AT² = 25 + 144 = 169 = OA². ✓
Answer: AT = 12 cm.

topics.topic_name: NUMBER OF TANGENTS FROM A POINT ON A CIRCLE

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
- LENGTH OF THE TANGENT from an external point P to a circle: The length of the segment from the external point P to the point of contact T (i.e., the distance PT).
- THEOREM 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: CASE 1 — Point INSIDE the circle: NO tangent can be drawn (every line through an interior point is a secant).
CASE 2 — Point ON the circle: Exactly ONE tangent can be drawn.
CASE 3 — Point OUTSIDE the circle: Exactly TWO tangents can be drawn.
From an external point, both tangents are of EQUAL LENGTH (Theorem 10.2).
In the proof of Theorem 10.2: RHS congruence is used.
The centre O lies on the ANGLE BISECTOR of the angle between the two tangents from an external point (i.e., OP bisects angle QPR).
Alternate proof of Theorem 10.2: PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR² → PQ = PR.
ACTIVITY 10.3.1: Tangents from Different Positions
AIM: To find the number of tangents from a point inside, on, and outside a circle.
MATERIALS: Paper, compass, ruler.
PROCEDURE:
Step 1: Draw a circle on paper. Take a point P inside it. Try drawing tangents through P.
Step 2: Take a point P on the circle. Draw tangents through P.
Step 3: Take a point P outside the circle. Draw tangents through P.
OBSERVATION:
Point inside: All lines through P intersect the circle at two points — no tangent possible.
Point on circle: Exactly one tangent.
Point outside: Exactly two tangents.
CONCLUSION:
Inside: 0 tangents. On circle: 1 tangent. Outside: 2 tangents.

sections.label: THEOREM 10.2:
sections.statement: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
sections.given: A circle with centre O, a point P lying outside the circle, two tangents PQ and PR where Q and R are points of contact.
proof: Step 1: In right triangles OQP and ORP:
angle OQP = 90° and angle ORP = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius, by Theorem 10.1)
Step 2: OQ = OR (radii of the same circle)
sections.hence_proved:
REMARKS:
1. Alternate proof: PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR² → PQ = PR.
2. angle OPQ = angle OPR, so OP is the angle bisector of angle QPR — the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.
EXAMPLES — TOPIC 10.3:
EXAMPLE 10.3.1: Chord of Larger Circle Bisected at Point of Contact
PROBLEM: Prove that in two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle, which touches the smaller circle, is bisected at the point of contact.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let two concentric circles C1 and C2 have centre O. Let AB be a chord of C1 that touches C2 at P.
Step 2: Join OP. AB is a tangent to C2 at P, and OP is its radius.
Step 3: By Theorem 10.1: OP ⊥ AB.
Step 4: AB is a chord of C1 and OP ⊥ AB. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
Step 5: Therefore: AP = BP.
ANSWER: The chord AB is bisected at P. HENCE PROVED.
EXAMPLE 10.3.2: Proving angle PTQ = 2 × angle OPQ
PROBLEM: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that angle PTQ = 2 × angle OPQ.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let angle PTQ = θ.
Step 2: By Theorem 10.2: TP = TQ → △TPQ is isosceles.
Step 3: Therefore: angle TPQ = angle TQP = (180° − θ)/2 = 90° − θ/2.
Step 4: By Theorem 10.1: angle OPT = 90°.
Step 5: angle OPQ = angle OPT − angle TPQ = 90° − (90° − θ/2) = θ/2.
Step 6: Therefore: angle PTQ = θ = 2 × angle OPQ.
ANSWER: angle PTQ = 2 × angle OPQ. HENCE PROVED.
EXAMPLE 10.3.3: Finding Length TP
PROBLEM: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T. Find the length TP.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Join OT. Let OT intersect PQ at R.
Step 2: △TPQ is isosceles (TP = TQ by Theorem 10.2) and TO bisects angle PTQ.
So OT ⊥ PQ and OT bisects PQ → PR = RQ = 4 cm.
Step 3: OR = √(OP² − PR²) = √(25 − 16) = √9 = 3 cm.
Step 4: In right △TRP and right △PRO:
angle TPR + angle RPO = 90° = angle TPR + angle PTR
So angle RPO = angle PTR.
Step 5: △TRP ~ △PRO (AA similarity).
TP/PO = RP/RO → TP/5 = 4/3 → TP = 20/3 cm.
Note: Alternate method using Pythagoras:
Let TP = x and TR = y.
x² = y² + 16  ...(1)  [Right △PRT]
x² + 25 = (y + 3)²  ...(2)  [Right △OPT]
From (2) − (1): 25 = 6y − 7 → y = 32/6 = 16/3
x² = (16/3)² + 16 = 256/9 + 144/9 = 400/9 → x = 20/3 cm.
ANSWER: TP = 20/3 cm.
EXERCISES — EXERCISE 10.2:

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.1:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: From a point Q, the length of the tangent to a circle is 24 cm and the distance of Q from the centre is 25 cm. The radius of the circle is:
(A) 7 cm  (B) 12 cm  (C) 15 cm  (D) 24.5 cm
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let radius = r. By Theorem 10.1: angle between tangent and radius = 90°.
Step 2: r² = OQ² − PQ² = 25² − 24² = 625 − 576 = 49 → r = 7 cm.
ANSWER: (A) 7 cm.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.2:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: In Fig. 10.11, TP and TQ are two tangents to a circle with centre O so that angle POQ = 110°. Then angle PTQ is:
(A) 60°  (B) 70°  (C) 80°  (D) 90°
SOLUTION:
Step 1: In quadrilateral TPOQ: angle TPO = angle TQO = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius).
Step 2: Sum of angles = 360°: angle PTQ + 90° + 110° + 90° = 360°.
Step 3: angle PTQ = 360° − 290° = 70°.
ANSWER: (B) 70°.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.3:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: If tangents PA and PB from a point P to a circle with centre O are inclined to each other at angle of 80°, then angle POA is:
(A) 50°  (B) 60°  (C) 70°  (D) 80°
SOLUTION:
Step 1: angle APB = 80° → angle APO = 40° (OP bisects angle APB).
Step 2: In right △OAP: angle OAP = 90°.
Step 3: angle POA = 180° − 90° − 40° = 50°.
ANSWER: (A) 50°.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.4:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let AB be the diameter of a circle with centre O. Let tangents at A and B be XAY and X'BY' respectively.
Step 2: By Theorem 10.1: OA ⊥ XAY → angle OAX = 90° and angle OAY = 90°.
Step 3: By Theorem 10.1: OB ⊥ X'BY' → angle OBX' = 90° and angle OBY' = 90°.
Step 4: OA and OB are along the same line (diameter AB).
Step 5: Both tangents are perpendicular to the same line AB.
ANSWER: Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel → tangents XAY ∥ X'BY'. HENCE PROVED.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.5:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Prove that the perpendicular at the point of contact to the tangent to a circle passes through the centre.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1, the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent at P.
Step 2: The perpendicular to the tangent at P is along the radius OP.
Step 3: The radius OP passes through the centre O.
ANSWER: Hence the perpendicular at the point of contact passes through the centre. HENCE PROVED.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.6:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: The length of a tangent from a point A at distance 5 cm from the centre of the circle is 4 cm. Find the radius of the circle.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: angle OAP = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius, Theorem 10.1).
Step 2: r² = OA² − PA² = 25 − 16 = 9 → r = 3 cm.
ANSWER: Radius = 3 cm.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.7:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Two concentric circles are of radii 5 cm and 3 cm. Find the length of the chord of the larger circle which touches the smaller circle.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let AB be the chord of the larger circle tangent to the smaller circle at P.
Step 2: By Example 10.3.1: OP ⊥ AB and P is the midpoint of AB.
Step 3: OP = 3 cm (radius of smaller circle), OA = 5 cm (radius of larger circle).
Step 4: AP = √(OA² − OP²) = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4 cm.
Step 5: AB = 2 × AP = 8 cm.
ANSWER: Length of chord = 8 cm.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.8:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle. Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let the circle touch AB at P, BC at Q, CD at R, DA at S.
Step 2: By Theorem 10.2 (tangents from external point are equal):
From A: AP = AS
From B: BP = BQ
From C: CR = CQ
From D: DR = DS
Step 3: AB + CD = (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + BQ) + (CQ + DS)
= (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ) = AD + BC.
ANSWER: AB + CD = AD + BC. HENCE PROVED.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.9:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: In Fig. 10.13, XY and X'Y' are two parallel tangents to a circle with centre O and another tangent AB with point of contact C intersecting XY at A and X'Y' at B. Prove that angle AOB = 90°.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Join OA and OB.
Step 2: In △OAP and △OAC (P = contact point on XY):
OA is common, AP = AC (tangents from A), angle OPA = angle OCA = 90°.
By RHS: △OAP ≅ △OAC → angle POA = angle COA.
So OA bisects angle PAC → angle OAP = angle OAC = (angle PAC)/2.
Step 3: Similarly: OB bisects angle QBC → angle OBQ = angle OBC.
Step 4: Since XY ∥ X'Y': angle PAB + angle QBA = 180° (co-interior angles).
Step 5: (angle PAC + angle CAB) + (angle QBC + angle CBA) = 180°.
Step 6: 2(angle OAC) + 2(angle OBC) = 180° (using angle bisector results).
angle OAC + angle OBC = 90°.
Step 7: In △AOB: angle AOB + angle OAB + angle OBA = 180°.
angle AOB = 180° − (angle OAC + angle OBC) = 180° − 90° = 90°.
ANSWER: angle AOB = 90°. HENCE PROVED.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.10:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Prove that the angle between the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle is supplementary to the angle subtended by the line-segment joining the points of contact at the centre.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let PA and PB be tangents from P, with A and B as contact points.
Step 2: In quadrilateral OAPB: angle OAP = 90°, angle OBP = 90°.
Step 3: Sum of all angles = 360°:
angle AOB + angle OAP + angle APB + angle OBP = 360°
angle AOB + 90° + angle APB + 90° = 360°
angle AOB + angle APB = 180°.
ANSWER: angle AOB + angle APB = 180° → they are supplementary. HENCE PROVED.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.11:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let ABCD be a parallelogram circumscribing a circle.
Step 2: By Exercise 10.2.8: AB + CD = AD + BC.
Step 3: In a parallelogram: AB = CD and AD = BC.
Step 4: Substituting: 2AB = 2AD → AB = AD.
Step 5: All four sides equal → ABCD is a rhombus.
ANSWER: The parallelogram ABCD is a rhombus. HENCE PROVED.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.12:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: A triangle ABC is drawn to circumscribe a circle of radius 4 cm such that BD = 8 cm and DC = 6 cm (segments of BC at point of contact D). Find the sides AB and AC.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let the circle touch AB at E and AC at F.
By Theorem 10.2: BD = BE = 8 cm, CD = CF = 6 cm, AE = AF = x.
Step 2: AB = x + 8, AC = x + 6, BC = 14 cm.
Step 3: s = (AB + BC + CA)/2 = (x + 8 + 14 + x + 6)/2 = x + 14.
Step 4: Area of △ABC = r × s = 4(x + 14).
Step 5: Also Area = √[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)] = √[(x+14)(x)(6)(8)] = √[48x(x+14)].
Step 6: Set equal: 4(x + 14) = √[48x(x + 14)]
16(x + 14)² = 48x(x + 14)
16(x + 14) = 48x
16x + 224 = 48x → 32x = 224 → x = 7 cm.
Step 7: AB = 7 + 8 = 15 cm; AC = 7 + 6 = 13 cm.
ANSWER: AB = 15 cm, AC = 13 cm.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.2.13:
sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Prove that opposite sides of a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle subtend supplementary angles at the centre of the circle.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Let ABCD circumscribe circle with centre O, touching at P (AB), Q (BC), R (CD), S (DA).
Step 2: Join OP, OQ, OR, OS.
Step 3: In △OAP and △OAS: AP = AS (tangents from A), OP = OS (radii), OA = OA (common).
By SSS: △OAP ≅ △OAS → angle AOP = angle AOS.
Step 4: Similarly: angle BOP = angle BOQ, angle COQ = angle COR, angle DOR = angle DOS.
Step 5: Total angles around O = 360°:
2(angle AOP + angle BOP + angle COQ + angle DOR) = 360° (but angle BOQ = angle BOP and angle COR = angle COQ)
(angle AOB) + (angle BOC) + (angle COD) + (angle DOA) = 360°.
Step 6: angle AOB + angle COD = (angle AOP + angle BOP) + (angle COR + angle DOR)
= (angle AOS + angle BOQ) + (angle COQ + angle DOS)
= (angle AOS + angle DOS) + (angle BOQ + angle COQ)
= angle DOA + angle BOC.
Step 7: Since angle AOB + angle BOC + angle COD + angle DOA = 360°:
2(angle AOB + angle COD) = 360° → angle AOB + angle COD = 180°.
ANSWER: Opposite sides subtend supplementary angles at the centre. HENCE PROVED.

items.question: State Theorem 10.2. What congruence rule is used in its proof?
items.answer:
Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
Congruence rule used: RHS (Right angle — Hypotenuse — Side).
In triangles OQP and ORP: angle OQP = angle ORP = 90° (Right angles), OP = OP (Hypotenuse), OQ = OR (Side — radii). By RHS: △OQP ≅ △ORP → PQ = PR.

items.question: How many tangents can be drawn from (i) a point inside, (ii) on, and (iii) outside the circle?
items.answer:
(i) Inside the circle: 0 tangents (every line through interior point is a secant).
(ii) On the circle: exactly 1 tangent.
(iii) Outside the circle: exactly 2 tangents (of equal length — Theorem 10.2).

items.question: What is the alternate proof of Theorem 10.2 using Pythagoras theorem?
items.answer:
By Theorem 10.1, angle OQP = angle ORP = 90°.
In right triangle OQP: PQ² = OP² − OQ².
In right triangle ORP: PR² = OP² − OR².
Since OQ = OR (radii): PQ² = PR² → PQ = PR.
Hence lengths of tangents from external point are equal.

items.question: From a point Q, tangent to a circle = 24 cm, distance from Q to centre = 25 cm. Find the radius.
items.answer:
By Theorem 10.1: angle OTQ = 90° (T = point of contact).
r² = OQ² − TQ² = 25² − 24² = 625 − 576 = 49.
r = 7 cm.
Answer: Radius = 7 cm.

3 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 3 questions:

items.question: Prove Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
items.answer:
Given: Circle with centre O, external point P, tangents PQ and PR (Q, R = points of contact).
To Prove: PQ = PR.
Construction: Join OP, OQ, OR.
Step 1: In △OQP and △ORP:
angle OQP = angle ORP = 90° (Theorem 10.1: tangent ⊥ radius).
OQ = OR (radii of same circle).
OP = OP (common hypotenuse).
Step 2: By RHS congruence: △OQP ≅ △ORP.
Step 3: By CPCT: PQ = PR. HENCE PROVED.

items.question: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn from external point T to a circle with centre O. Angle PTQ = 70°. Find angle POQ and angle OPT.
items.answer:
Step 1: In quadrilateral TPOQ: angle TPO = angle TQO = 90° (Theorem 10.1).
angle PTQ + angle TPO + angle POQ + angle TQO = 360°.
70° + 90° + angle POQ + 90° = 360°.
angle POQ = 110°.
Step 2: OT bisects angle PTQ (by Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ → isosceles △TPQ).
angle OTP = 70°/2 = 35°.
Step 3: In right triangle OPT: angle OPT = 90° (Theorem 10.1).
angle POT = 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°.
Answer: angle POQ = 110°. angle OPT = 90°.

items.question: A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm, CD = 4 cm. Find AD. State the theorem used.
items.answer:
Theorem used: For a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle: AB + CD = AD + BC.
Step 1: This follows from Theorem 10.2 — tangents from each vertex are equal.
From each vertex: the two tangent lengths to the circle are equal.
Step 2: AB + CD = AD + BC.
6 + 4 = AD + 7.
10 = AD + 7.
Step 3: AD = 3 cm.
Answer: AD = 3 cm.

---

4 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 4 questions:

items.question: Prove: In two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle which touches the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact.
items.answer:
Given: Concentric circles C1 (larger, radius R) and C2 (smaller, radius r), common centre O. Chord AB of C1 is tangent to C2 at P.
To Prove: AP = BP.
Construction: Join OP.
Proof:
Step 1: AB is a tangent to C2 at P. OP is the radius of C2 to the point of contact P.
Step 2: By Theorem 10.1: OP ⊥ AB.
Step 3: OP is perpendicular to chord AB of circle C1 from centre O.
Step 4: By the property "perpendicular from centre to chord bisects the chord": AP = BP.
HENCE PROVED.

items.question: Prove: A quadrilateral ABCD drawn to circumscribe a circle satisfies AB + CD = AD + BC.
items.answer:
Given: ABCD circumscribes a circle. Circle touches AB at P, BC at Q, CD at R, DA at S.
To Prove: AB + CD = AD + BC.
Proof:
Step 1: From vertex A: AP = AS (Theorem 10.2)  ...(1)
Step 2: From vertex B: BP = BQ (Theorem 10.2)  ...(2)
Step 3: From vertex C: CQ = CR (Theorem 10.2)  ...(3)
Step 4: From vertex D: DR = DS (Theorem 10.2)  ...(4)
Step 5: Adding (1)+(2)+(3)+(4):
(AP + BP) + (CQ + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)
AB + CD = AD + BC. HENCE PROVED.

items.question: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. Tangents at P and Q meet at T. Find TP.
items.answer:
Given: Chord PQ = 8 cm, radius OP = OQ = 5 cm, tangents at P and Q meet at T.
Step 1: By Theorem 10.2: TP = TQ. Let OT meet PQ at R.
OT ⊥ PQ and R is midpoint of PQ → PR = 4 cm.
Step 2: In right triangle OPR:
OR = √(OP² − PR²) = √(25 − 16) = 3 cm.
Step 3: Let TR = y, TP = x.
In right △TPR: x² = y² + 16  ...(1)
In right △OPT: x² + 25 = (y + 3)²  ...(2)
Step 4: (2) − (1): 25 = 6y − 7 → y = 32/6 = 16/3.
Step 5: x² = (16/3)² + 16 = 256/9 + 144/9 = 400/9 → x = 20/3 cm.
Answer: TP = 20/3 cm.

items.question: Prove: If tangents PA and PB are drawn from external point P, then angle AOB + angle APB = 180°. Find angle AOB if angle APB = 60°.
items.answer:
Given: Circle with centre O, external point P, tangents PA and PB (A, B = points of contact).
To Prove: angle AOB + angle APB = 180°.
Proof:
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1: angle OAP = 90° and angle OBP = 90°.
Step 2: In quadrilateral OAPB:
angle AOB + angle OAP + angle APB + angle OBP = 360°.
angle AOB + 90° + angle APB + 90° = 360°.
Step 3: angle AOB + angle APB = 180°. HENCE PROVED.

Application: If angle APB = 60°:
angle AOB = 180° − 60° = 120°.
Answer: angle AOB = 120°.

---

5 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 1 question:

PART A — Full Proof of Theorem 10.2:

Statement: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
Given: Circle with centre O. P is outside the circle. PQ and PR are tangents from P, touching the circle at Q and R respectively.
To Prove: PQ = PR.
Construction: Join OP, OQ, OR.

Step 1: In right triangle OQP:
angle OQP = 90° (by Theorem 10.1 — tangent ⊥ radius at Q).
OP is the hypotenuse. OQ = radius.
Step 2: In right triangle ORP:
angle ORP = 90° (by Theorem 10.1 — tangent ⊥ radius at R).
OP is the hypotenuse (same). OR = OQ = radius of same circle.
Step 3: Comparing △OQP and △ORP:
angle OQP = angle ORP = 90°  (Right angles)
OP = OP                       (Common hypotenuse)
OQ = OR                       (Radii of same circle)
Step 4: By RHS congruence rule: △OQP ≅ △ORP.
Step 5: By CPCT: PQ = PR. HENCE PROVED.

Remark: From CPCT, angle OPQ = angle OPR → OP bisects angle QPR.
The centre O lies on the angle bisector of the angle between the two tangents from P.
Alternate proof: PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR² → PQ = PR.

---

PART B — Finding AB and AC:

Given: Triangle ABC circumscribes circle (radius r = 4 cm). D is point of contact on BC. BD = 8 cm, DC = 6 cm.
Let circle touch AB at E, AC at F. Let AE = AF = x.

Step 1: By Theorem 10.2:
From B: BD = BE = 8 cm.
From C: CD = CF = 6 cm.
AB = x + 8,  AC = x + 6,  BC = 14 cm.

Step 2: Semi-perimeter:
s = (AB + BC + CA)/2 = (x + 8 + 14 + x + 6)/2 = x + 14.

Step 3: Area by inradius formula:
Area = r × s = 4(x + 14)  ...(i)

Step 4: Area by Heron's formula:
s − AB = 6,  s − BC = x,  s − CA = 8.
Area = √[(x+14)(6)(x)(8)] = √[48x(x+14)]  ...(ii)

Step 5: From (i) = (ii):
4(x + 14) = √[48x(x + 14)]
Squaring: 16(x + 14)² = 48x(x + 14)
16(x + 14) = 48x
16x + 224 = 48x → 32x = 224 → x = 7 cm.

Step 6: AB = 7 + 8 = 15 cm.  AC = 7 + 6 = 13 cm.
Answer: AB = 15 cm and AC = 13 cm.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text: - This section summarises all key results studied in Chapter 10: Circles.

sections.label: Key Points — Summary of Chapter 10:
points: 1. The meaning of a TANGENT to a circle: a line that intersects the circle at exactly one point called the POINT OF CONTACT.
2. THEOREM 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
3. THEOREM 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
KEY RESULTS TO REMEMBER:
From a point INSIDE the circle: 0 tangents.
From a point ON the circle: 1 tangent.
From a point OUTSIDE the circle: 2 tangents (equal in length).
Tangent ⊥ Radius at point of contact.
Centre lies on the angle bisector of the two tangents from an external point.
In a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle: AB + CD = AD + BC.
A parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a RHOMBUS.
In two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle that is tangent to the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact.
angle PTQ + angle POQ = 180° (for two tangents from external point T).
